THE HANDOFF'S ACCOUNT OF THE UNRESOLVED ODDS NAMES WAS WRONG. It recorded '36 unresolved names, ~14 are alias-map gaps'. There is no alias map, and the failures are structural, not lexical. _PlayerNameIndex has three rungs; rung 2 matches the LAST token of the odds name against FPL web_name tokens. But the odds feed supplies a player's FULL LEGAL name while FPL's web_name is frequently a MONONYM or short form that is not the last token: 'Murillo Santiago Costa dos Santos' is FPL's 'Murillo' (element 472, first='Murillo' second='Costa dos Santos'), 'Ruben Dias' is 'Rúben' (390), 'Estevao Oliveira Goncalves' is 'Estêvão' (157), 'Matheus Luiz Nunes' is 'Matheus N.' (389). Hyphenated surnames fail from the other side: the FPL index splits its own names on hyphens but 'Emile Smith-Rowe' arrives as ONE trailing token. Separately, ß does NOT decompose under NFKD, so FPL's 'Groß' indexed as 'groß' and could never meet the feed's 'Gross'. Diagnosed by running the real resolver over the real capture and classifying every failure, not by reading the code.

Added rung 3 to _PlayerNameIndex.resolve plus ß->ss in _LATIN_TRANSLITERATION. Rung 3 tries EVERY token (splitting on hyphens as well as spaces, dropping tokens under 4 chars so particles like dos/da/ta and initials add no collision surface) and accepts only if the union across tokens is a SINGLE element, inside the existing two-squad candidate pool. detail: UNSTANDARDISED FEATURES SILENTLY BREAK A GRADIENT-BASED GLM FIT UNDER A SHARED l2_penalty CONVENTION, EVEN WHEN L-BFGS-B REPORTS GENUINE CONVERGENCE. Fitting the attacking-involvement Binomial-share regression at l2_penalty=1.0 (the DC/minutes shared default) on the real store converged to a REAL stationary point (gradient norm ~1e-5, not a premature stop) that was nonetheless football-nonsensical: games_played_this_season (raw range 0..37) read as the single largest-magnitude coefficient, every player_trailing_{xg,goals}_* coefficient sat under 0.002, and position=FWD read NEGATIVE for the goals model. Mechanism: a fixed L2 penalty charges the same quadratic cost per unit of beta regardless of what a unit buys on that feature's own scale -- a two-orders-of-magnitude scale gap (0..37 vs 0..2) lets the large-scale, less-informative feature move eta cheaply while the small-scale, genuinely informative features get crushed toward zero. Standardising every numeric column (z-score, frozen at fit time in AttackingFeatureSpec, applied identically at predict time) plus lowering l2_penalty to 0.01 (swept against the real store, gate first passes at 0.015) fixed it -- see docs/wiki/model-attacking.md §6-7 for the full sweep table. DC and minutes happened not to hit this because their own feature sets are more homogeneously scaled; any FUTURE Phase 2 model mixing count features (0..37 range) with rate features (0..2 range) under a shared l2_penalty=1.0 convention should check its own feature-scale spread rather than assuming the DC/minutes default transfers -- worth a blueprint/wiki note for the next model builder.

claim: Bonus is a rank-within-fixture phenomenon coupling every player in a fixture's BPS draws -- a per-player independent PMF (the shape every other Phase 2 model in this project uses) cannot represent this, because summing independent per-player P(bonus=k) across a fixture does not respect the fixture-total constraint (exactly 6, or a tie-inflated 7/8/9). predict_bonus_pmfs_for_fixture therefore takes a WHOLE FIXTURE (Sequence[BonusPlayerInput]) and returns one PMF per player from the SAME seeded Monte Carlo draw -- a deliberate, documented deviation from every sibling module's per-player predict_*_pmf(...) signature. Any future model whose target is itself a multi-entity joint outcome (e.g. captaincy EO, which is normalised across an entire gameweek's entry pool) should expect the same shape mismatch against the per-player PMF convention, not force-fit it.
source: design work this session, src/fplai/models/bonus.py module docstring

claim: BPS is NOT sign-constrained (real store range -25..128: cards/missed penalties/own goals push it negative), so DC's multiplicative log(minutes/90) offset and attacking's minutes_frac*sigmoid(...) parametrisation both structurally do not apply -- a multiplicative minutes term forces bps->0 unconditionally as minutes shrinks, which is wrong in principle even though correct in the modal case, and is nonsensical for a genuinely negative predicted mean. bonus.py instead puts minutes_frac into the standardised feature vector as an ordinary regression feature, which forces a second deviation from house convention: zero-minute rows must be INCLUDED in the fit (not filtered out the way DC/attacking filter minutes>0), both because there is no log(0) constraint to avoid and because the joint fixture simulation needs the true full competitive universe (verified: 96,717/96,729 zero-minute rows carry bps=0, i.e. 99.99%). A future real-valued (sign-unconstrained) target should not inherit the multiplicative-offset convention by default -- check the target's own sign constraint first.
source: design work this session, src/fplai/models/bonus.py module docstring 'Why minutes_frac is a feature, not an offset'

claim: Closed-form ridge regression (beta = (X^T X/n + l2*I)^-1 * X^T y/n) is available whenever the target is genuinely real-valued (no count/probability link function needed) and sidesteps the WHOLE class of bug fplai.models.attacking paid for (l2_penalty=1.0 on an unstandardised matrix converging L-BFGS-B to a real-but-nonsensical stationary point) -- not just the scale-transfer half (still requires feature standardisation) but the CONVERGENCE half too, since a convex quadratic has a unique closed-form minimiser with no iteration, no maxiter, no 'did not converge cleanly' path. Cross-checked in tests/test_bonus.py both against its own zero-gradient condition and an independent scipy.optimize.minimize run. Worth using for any future real-valued-target module rather than defaulting to L-BFGS-B out of habit.

detail: TIMEZONE DEFECT IN THE PL ADAPTER, FOUND BY MEASUREMENT WHILE DE-RISKING THE CARDS JOIN -- and it is a leakage-direction bug, not just a join nuisance. The PL API returns a fixture kickoff as a bare wall-clock string with NO offset ('2025-08-15 20:00:00') and it is EUROPE/LONDON, not UTC; providers/pl.py did datetime.strptime(...) and stored it as though it were UTC. Evidence: joining PL fixtures to vaastav's own FPL-sourced kickoff_time (explicitly Z) on (away_team_code, kickoff) matched only 223 of 375 fixtures in 2025-26; the delta on the rest was EXACTLY -60 minutes and split perfectly on the calendar -- 0 minutes in Nov-Mar (GMT), -60 in Apr/May/Aug/Sep (BST), October straddling the changeover. Two independent sources agreeing all winter and differing by precisely one hour all summer is conclusive. IMPACT BEYOND THE JOIN: fplai.backfill._valid_at_for anchors lineups, substitutions, team_match_stats AND officials on this same kickoff, so every BST row's valid_at was one hour EARLY -- and blueprint 3.2 is explicit that understating how early a fact became true is merely conservative while OVERSTATING it is the leakage direction. Affected roughly 163,000 rows already written. Fixed at the single parse site with a documented Europe/London -> tz-naive UTC conversion; regression test proved to fail first, covering both sides of the autumn changeover so an 'April to October' rule-of-thumb implementation cannot pass it.

Re-ingesting all five per-match PL capabilities for 2020-2025 with corrected kickoffs, into a SEPARATE checkpoint (data/backfill/pl_api_tzfix.jsonl) so the original is left untouched rather than moved or deleted. Responses come from the transport cache, so this costs no new API requests -- the rate policy is respected by construction. The store is append-only and bitemporal, so the corrected rows land as NEW observations and as_of()/effective_at() resolve to them; the wrong rows remain in history where they belong rather than being rewritten, which is the whole point of the design.

ARCHITECT REJECTS ONE ACCEPTANCE IN THE CALIBRATION REPORT, on the report's OWN argument. It accepts bonus's underconfident departures (slopes 1.089-2.219) partly because 'underconfident is the SAFER direction for an optimiser to inherit than cards' overconfident direction -- a PMF under-claiming its certainty costs less than one that over-claims it'. That argument is correct. But the report then accepts cards NONE and YELLOW, which are OVERCONFIDENT (slopes 0.592 and 0.630, CIs [0.554,0.629] and [0.591,0.669], nowhere near 1), with the milder justification that ECE is low and ranking is usable. By its own reasoning the dangerous direction deserves LESS tolerance, not equal tolerance. And the remedy is known to work in this codebase: the minutes model went slope 1.114 -> 0.972 and ECE 0.0507 -> 0.0131 with a nested out-of-sample isotonic layer. Accepting a defect we already know how to fix, in the direction the report itself calls the costly one, is deferral dressed as a decision. RULING: E5 passes -- every outcome beats both baselines and the gate's stated criteria are met -- but cards NONE/YELLOW carry a BLOCKING CONDITION ON PHASE 3: an isotonic layer before the optimiser consumes them. Bonus's underconfidence may ride, being the safe direction with a wide baseline margin.

METHODOLOGICAL FINDING WORTH PROMOTING BEYOND THIS PROJECT'S CALIBRATION WORK: EQUAL-WIDTH ECE UNDER-REPORTS A DEPARTURE CONCENTRATED IN A SPARSE HIGH-PROBABILITY TAIL. Bonus's quantile-binned ECE is materially larger than its equal-width ECE on EVERY one of its four outcomes (e.g. outcome 0: 0.0091 width vs 0.0163 quantile; outcome 3: 0.0002 vs 0.0070). The equal-width binning concentrates a rare class's rows into low-probability bins and dilutes exactly the region where the miscalibration lives. This SETTLES the ECE-versus-slope disagreement HANDOFF logged as blocking: the slope's signal was correct and ECE's binning was the misleading one. It is also the empirical justification for the blueprint amendment made hours earlier, which asserted on principle that ECE must not arbitrate -- there is now evidence for WHY, not just an argument. Any future reliability work in this codebase should report BOTH binnings, and a single-binning ECE should be treated as an incomplete measurement.
